newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lamfalussy-full access to TARGET could harm policy.
newsitem.headline: Lamfalussy-full access to TARGET could harm policy.

text.p: Alexandre Lamfalussy, head of the European Monetary Institute, said on Monday that the provision of unlimited intraday euro credit to non-euro countries could lead to a disruption of European monetary policy.

Speaking to reporters at Frankfurt's International Business Journalists' Forum, Lamfalussy said a decision to offer full participation in the TARGET payments system to countries that remained outside could increase demand for Euros.
This in turn would bring an additional uncertainty to the pattern of demand for the fledgling currency from its creation in 1999, he said.
TARGET is the acronym for the cross-border payment system of the future European Central Bank, the successor to the EMI, which will manage European monetary policy under a single currency.

At issue is the question of whether national central banks in countries that do not give up their own currencies in 1999 should be given full access to the system, which would allow them to grant intra-day and overnight euro credits in TARGET.

Britain, which is not expected to join the single currency in 1999 for political reasons, has lobbied hard for full access to TARGET, fearing that partial exclusion will hurt London's standing as a financial centre.
An EMI report produced earlier this month floated the idea of giving such countries only limited access to the system with the aim of preventing them holding overnight credits.

Lamfalussy said that, although it would be optimal for the functioning of the individual countries' gross payment (RTGS) systems for them to have unlimited access to credits, it could pose problems if this were given in such cases.
"There is a problem area when intra-day credit extends into overnight," Lamfalussy said. "That could have a more lasting impact on money markets."

Taking note of the concerns of countries that may be left out of the EMU in the first round in 1999, Lamfalussy said, however, that there were only two clear cases of countries that knew they would be excluded -- Britain and Denmark.
"Only two countries regard themselves as either certain or potential outs," he said. "No other country is in the position setting out to defend the position of outsider.
He said one problem with full access to TARGET for such countries lay in the increased demand for money that would be created as a result of blanket access for non-EMU countries.

This could distort money flows, which will be hard to assess anyway in the first few years of the euro's life, he added, making it even harder for the European central bank to learn much from monetary aggregate figures.

"My concern is that, in the running-in period for the euro, it will be hard to asses the demand," he said. "If at the same time the use of the euro develops outside the area in a totally unpredictable way then the indicator value of money supply becomes even more difficult to grasp," he said.

The EMI said in a recent report that the ECB could use either monetary or inflation targets to guide its monetary policy, but warned that uncertainty over money demand patterns could be a problem for monetary policy targeting.
